**February 29, 1960 — a Monday, and a date that exists only once every four years**

You did not have a birthday in 1961, 1962, or 1963. The calendar simply did not produce your date. In 66 years of life, you have had 16 actual birthdays on February 29 — the most recent in 2024, when you turned 64 on your true date. The next will arrive on February 29, 2028. Legally and culturally, the question of when a leap-day person officially turns a year older has been answered differently by jurisdictions, employers, and school systems across the world. The rarity is not merely whimsical: you were born on a date that appears only in years divisible by four — which themselves carry a particular weight. Every true birthday of your life has coincided with an Olympic year and an American presidential election year. The calendar chose its moments carefully.

---

**The Agadir earthquake: the exact day you were born**

In the early hours of February 29, 1960, a powerful earthquake struck Agadir, Morocco, killing an estimated 12,000 to 15,000 people — roughly a third of the city's entire population. The tremor was not extraordinary by Richter scale standards, but Agadir's buildings were not built to withstand it: the old kasbah and the newer European quarter collapsed together. The city had to be largely abandoned and rebuilt on a new site. It remains one of the deadliest natural disasters of 20th-century Africa. The world you entered on February 29, 1960 included that catastrophe occurring at the same moment you arrived.

---

**1960: the year that made the 1960s**

The decade that shaped your entire upbringing was just beginning. Eisenhower had weeks left in his presidency. John F. Kennedy had announced his candidacy in January and was campaigning through the New Hampshire primary. The Space Race was in full sprint — Soviet and American engineers racing toward the Moon, shaping entire federal budgets and national identities. The first televised presidential debate, Kennedy versus Nixon in September 1960, would take place when you were seven months old and transform American democracy in ways that have never reversed. The 1960s are often remembered as if they began in 1963 or 1964, but the forces that made them were already in motion the week you were born.

---

**Twenty-eight days before you were born: Greensboro**

On February 1, 1960 — 28 days before your birth — four Black college students sat at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and refused to leave when denied service. The sit-in movement that followed spread to dozens of cities within weeks. The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee was founded by summer. By the time you were four, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 had passed. The movement was already in motion when you were born, but it was moving fast, and the entire arc of your childhood unfolded alongside it.

---

**±30 days: Sharpeville**

Twenty-one days after your birth, on March 21, 1960, South African police opened fire on a crowd gathered peacefully in Sharpeville to protest the apartheid pass laws. Sixty-nine people were killed; most were shot in the back. The Sharpeville Massacre shocked the world, hardened international opinion against the apartheid regime, triggered a state of emergency in South Africa, and led directly to the banning of the African National Congress. March 21 is now observed as the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. The date you were born sits almost exactly between the Greensboro sit-ins and Sharpeville — between the American civil rights movement reaching critical mass and the global anti-apartheid movement receiving its defining wound.

---

**The arc of 66 years**

You were born into a world where the Cold War was the structural fact of political life, where civil rights were still legally contested in a wealthy democracy, where computers occupied government buildings, and where a transatlantic phone call required advance arrangement and significant expense.

In 66 years: Kennedy was elected and assassinated. The Civil Rights Act passed. Vietnam began and ended. Humans walked on the Moon. The Berlin Wall rose and fell. The Soviet Union dissolved. Apartheid ended. The personal computer arrived. The internet connected the world. The smartphone placed the sum of human knowledge in a pocket.

And through all of it: 16 actual birthdays on your date. The calendar offered them sparingly, at four-year intervals — always in Olympic years, always in presidential election years, always in years the world was already marking as significant. Most people measure their lives in annual rings. You have always had a slightly different relationship with time.
